statement: Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to present AB 2379 to safeguard the constitutional rights of family childcare providers. I represent a large immigrant community in Southeast Los Angeles. For nearly a year, communities like mine have been under attack and living in fear. Inhumane deportation rates have spread fear across our communities, disrupted our workforce, and threatened access to vital childcare services for both families and providers. We must take legislative action to better protect our communities and access to essential services like childcare.

speaker: José Solache
statement: Childcare providers responsible for taking care of our children, statewide, deserve access to tools and resources needed to protect themselves and our children. AB 2379 ensures license and—license-exempt family childcare providers are informed with the constitutional rights when confronted by immigration enforcement. The bill requires the Department of Social Services to notify providers of the Fourth Amendment protections until they coordinate accessible multilingual training. The training will ensure providers understand the rights regarding searches, seizures, arrests, and detentions in their homes.

statement: The bill will help childcare pro open—childcare doors open—and safe from intimidation, misinformation, and unlawful searches or arrest when confronted by immigration enforcement.

My parents came to this country from Leon, Guanajuato to build a better life to our—of our family. speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: During the COVID pandemic, I spent more than four hours on hold at one point trying to get medication for my 98 year old mother. speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: Customers need to be able to promptly fill a medication to prevent their utilities from getting shut off and access sensitive information for scheduling purposes.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: AB 1609 ensures meaningful access to live assistance by requiring that large businesses offer access to a live human representative during business hours, limiting hold times after a telephonic call or online customer service inquiry is answered, requiring transparency, including clear disclosure of AI use and prohibiting AI from being presented as human, and prominently displaying a phone number if one is made available for live assistance. AB 1609 does not ban automation. Under this bill, businesses may continue using AI and automated systems.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: However, automation cannot replace real and vital workers or be used as a barrier to the prevents people from reaching prompt help when they need it.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur

statement: Just a moment, madam majority leader. Thank you, members. Madam majority leader, you may open on the measure.

statement: Thank you, mister speaker and members. First, I want to thank all of my colleagues who took the time to connect with me and discuss this bill. From the bottom of my heart, thank you. And you all know those of you that have spent the spend the time on this bill. You know, I know many of you have heard I have this small district bill.

speaker: Cecilia Aguiar-Curry
statement: But in all seriousness, this is a complex but critically important issue. California Cartwright Act is our state's primary antitrust law. But it contains a major loophole. If two businesses conspire to undercut competition, that's illegal. That kind of anti competitive conduct hurts competitors, consumers, and workers.

speaker: Cecilia Aguiar-Curry
statement: It hurts everyone except the companies who rig the system. But if one dominant company takes the same actions and causes the same harm, the Cartwright Act does not cover it. That does not make sense. And federal law and 45 states agree. Both federal law and the vast majority of other states recognize that one dominant company can be just as harmful as two companies acting together.

speaker: Cecilia Aguiar-Curry
statement: This conversation is especially important now because consolidation has touched nearly every part of our economy. Since the 1990s, more than 75% of US industries have experienced increased market concentration. That means higher prices, fewer choices, fewer opportunities for job creators to start small businesses, and suppressed wages for working families. I took on this issue because one of my proudest accomplishments as the mayor of Winters was helping build a thriving main street full of successful and engaged small businesses.

speaker: Cecilia Aguiar-Curry
statement: Today, many of those businesses are struggling to compete as suppliers disappear and markets become more concentrated.

speaker: Cecilia Aguiar-Curry
statement: I hear from restaurant owners facing higher supply costs and fewer choices. I see it on my family farm when suppliers no longer exist. This issue is is economy wide, and the legislature recognized that when we passed a bipartisan resolution directing the California Law Revision Commission to study the Cartwright Act. The commission spent more than three years. They studied this issue with 8 working groups of legal experts, economists, and stakeholders.

speaker: Cecilia Aguiar-Curry
statement: They held 18 public meetings, receiving thousands of public comments, and draft a proposal that works within California's existing antitrust framework. This bill does not punish success. It does not punish corporate growth. AB 1776 is about making sure that when a dominant company abuses its power to shut out competition and harm consumers, workers, and small businesses, California has the tools to respond. This bill protects free and fair competition and helps ensure the California marketplace works for everyone.

speaker: Cecilia Aguiar-Curry
statement: I know I know we have much more to do. But without a single proposed amendment from the major opponents, we have already taken significant amendments to the bill based on your feedback, colleagues. Your feedback. I exempted small businesses and added strong guardrails. And I am committing to you today to remove section three from the bill and move a narrowed down version from statutory to intent language in Section one.

speaker: Cecilia Aguiar-Curry
statement: I ask that you let me continue that work. Thank you very much.

speaker: Ash Kalra
statement: The law revision commission in January this year released the proposal to reform the Cartwright Act to addressing all firm conduct, And this bill would enact those recommendations and use somewhat of a hybrid approach, which will really honor many, many years of case law, recognizing that California's anti competition laws are and should continue to be even stronger than federal regulations.

speaker: Ash Kalra
statement: But the reality is that even when you think about the the two party conduct rule, that was made during a time prior to e-commerce, prior to how we conduct our business these days, and prior to the ability that exists now for one company to have so much power over our market, that these revisions are so critical in order to ensure that California consumers and small businesses have an opportunity to have a fair shot of participating in the current modern economy.

speaker: Ash Kalra
statement: And by ensuring that by allowing this bill to move forward, we're making it very clear that California, first of all, is not gonna fall behind so many other states that have already taken action, but that California honestly should be a leader on this. speaker: Ash Kalra
statement: I think it's really not that complicated of a piece of legislation, and and it's pretty straightforward in what it's trying to achieve in ensuring that we don't allow any actors to have such inordinate influence over our markets, that not only does it have an anti competitive impact on other businesses in the market, but it also doesn't shut out the opportunity for consumers to have a genuine real choice when they're making their decisions on quality of life issues.

speaker: Ash Kalra
statement: So I respectfully ask for an aye vote, and, again, I commend the author for her stalwart work on this.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: We need to make sure that our laws are make are protecting California consumers, making sure that prices are going down, that we're actually advancing competition and not thwarting it.

statement: Mister speaker, members, I'm ready this time. I rise to present AB 1740 sponsored by the city of Santa Monica and Streets for All. Since the passage of the California Coastal Act of 1976, the Coastal Commission has done paramount work to advance twin objectives, safeguarding our natural resources and ensuring equitable public access to the coast.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: Yet in fifty years since the Coastal Act was passed, much has changed in California.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: While public access was one defined by roads and parking lots, today cars are a part of an equation in some of our denser urban coastal cities, an equation that now includes trains, buses, bike lanes, and walkable streets. Yet in these cities, the commission often can be seen treating built out urban areas as if they were undeveloped coastline.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: In places like Downtown Santa Monica, which I represent, routine actions such as changing the use of a small building or constructing already approved housing that has absolutely no impact on sensitive resources or other precious coastal, resources often requires lengthy coastal commission approvals that often defeat really good proposals. If these activities were taking place in a sensitive ecosystem, they might pose an a real environmental threat. But in a built out city, we need to treat these things differently.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: The lengthy delays caused by the coastal commission's reviews sometimes do have real impact on a city, on residents and businesses who wait months and even years for approvals that have no negative impacts. I could provide a number of real world examples of this happening in my city and in others. The original version of this bill addressed these challenges through exemptions to the Coastal Act for a select group of cities that met standards around public access, transit, and greenhouse gas reduction.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: However, the bill before you today represents an alternative approach, the results of a positive productive negotiations between and among the Coastal Commission and the city of Santa Monica in my office. This past week, after decades without a local coastal program, Santa Monica and the Coastal Commission agreed on a memorandum of understanding to guide LCP negotiations with both sides saying completion within eighteen months is feasible.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: Santa Monica City council voted seven to o to approve that MOU last night. So AB 1740 has already served as a catalyst pushing both sides to the table. Amendments taken last week reframe, the previous broad permit exemptions with a deadline and incentive framework tied to the city of Santa Monica's LCP completion. And while discussions with the Coastal Commission are in progress, and we still have work to address all of their concerns, the bill moves forward the the approach that they requested.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: The bill most importantly requires development and certification of a local coastal plan for the city of Santa Monica in coordination with the Coastal Commission.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: The bill now offers immediate interim exemptions, which are shorter and smaller than what was approved through committees last week prior to LCP certification for changes of use and and and minor interior and exterior renovations of small buildings, minor projects to improve ADA compliance, and EV charging station deployment. At the same time, the bill incentivizes the commission to complete the LCP in a reasonable but timely fashion.

speaker: Rick Chavez Zbur
statement: The bill concurrently provides for SMITE climate strategies by giving the Coastal Commission new tools to support and improve faster investments in transit, bike lanes, and pedestrian transportation across the entire state. The bill rewards a good faith effort between the Coastal Commission and the city of Santa Monica, and it brings both parties to the table, supports the city of Santa Monica in certifying an LCP that will preserve the California Coastal Commission's authority and ability to protect beaches and coastal resources from activities that threaten sensitive resources.

statement: Well, thank you, mister speaker. Today today, I rise to present AB 1881, the California Indian Freedom Act of 2026. It seeks to ensure that California Indians can freely practice their religions and spiritual traditions on state public lands. As I have continuously echoed on this floor, California is home to the largest population of Native Americans in The United States, each with its own distinct culture and religion that has predated statehood.

speaker: James Ramos
statement: Yet for centuries, there has been a long standing policy in this country and in this state that has allowed for the suppression of tribal spirituality and cultural expressions in an effort to assimilate the Indians by force using slogans like kill the Indian and save the man.

speaker: James Ramos
statement: In fact, California was home to 13 federal Indian boarding schools that abducted native children from their families, punish them for speaking their language, and prohibited them from practicing their spiritual practices. These boarding schools resulted in generational trauma that continues to plague and impact tribal communities to this day. Unfortunately, the legacy of Indian assimilation and cultural suppression still shapes present day policy. Sacred sites are still being desecrated, developed, or made inaccessible.

speaker: James Ramos
statement: Many tribes remain separated from their cultural items and their ancestors that still remain on shelves at universities in the state of California.

speaker: James Ramos
statement: Tribal members are routinely questioned or harassed for wearing regalia or carrying ceremonial items in public spaces. Native students and their families still face obstacles or prohibitions on wearing regalia at graduation ceremonies despite federal and state statutory protections that this body has approved. These are not isolated incidents. They are a direct result of state and federal policies that sought to erase Native American identity and religion.

speaker: James Ramos
statement: AB 1881 aims to afford Native Americans the same level of protection for their faith as we do for other religions in this country and in the state of California.

speaker: James Ramos
statement: The ability for many tribal communities through their faith depends on access to sacred sites to gather traditional plants and foods and enjoy the freedom to use their ceremonial items without being questioned every step of the way. AB 1881 establishes clear, enforceable standards that no state agency may substantially burden a California tribe's right to religious practice unless the state can demonstrate a compelling interest in doing so. Even then, it must do so by the least restrictive means possible.

speaker: James Ramos
statement: The bill ensures that state agencies allow access to sacred sites on state lands and permit gathering of traditional plants, foods, and other materials and essentials to tribal religious practices. The bill further protects the handling of sacred items and Regala, even on state grounds, including here at the state capitol.

speaker: Chris Ward
statement: And simply put, companies are using what they know about you, who you are, and where you go, and how much you spend, and even your location to decide how much to charge you. speaker: Chris Ward

speaker: Nick Schultz

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: But I do rise to present AB 1603, and I'd like to note that should the bill pass off the floor today, I commit to amending the bill in the Senate to remove any language that bans a certain set of PFAS pesticides in 2030, as well as a ban on any remaining PFAS pesticides in 2035. Therefore, and this is the operative part, the bill will no longer ban any PFAS pesticides used in the state of California today.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: After amendments are made, AB 1603 will prohibit state approvals of new pesticides containing PFAS starting in January. However, this would not prohibit approval of applications that are in possession and being processed by DPR before that deadline.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: In addition, the bill would designate all PFAS pesticide as restricted materials and therefore require use of those pesticides to be publicly disclosed and permitted by county agricultural commissioners starting in 2028. Those are the amendments. Why did I bring this bill forward? Well, for those of you who don't know, PFAS is a large class of chemicals that are used in many consumer products and industries because they are long lasting and waterproof.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: And especially in the agricultural context, I understand that those properties can be very helpful. However, there are also associated with those products a number of serious human health effects that can not only impact our bodies, but build up in water and soil, and they are perpetual.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: They don't go away. Because of PFAS very problematic properties, the California legislature, as you all well know, has acted in recent years to prohibit their use in many consumer products, including textiles, food packaging, and cosmetics.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: And state officials have limited the use of PFAS in carpets and upholstery and are about to regulate PFAS in cleaners. But I was shocked to learn that the state, in my view, is not doing anything about PFAS containing pesticides that are regularly used on California crops.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: And I was more shocked to learn that PFAS pesticides are present on the fruits and vegetables that we feed our families. For example, strawberries, a fruit known for heavy pesticide use, can contain the residue of 10 different PFAS pesticides.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: And according to a recent Environmental Working Group analysis, California currently allows 53 PFAS pesticides to be used on California grown crops, and more than 2.5 million pounds of this PFAS is deposited on California agriculture and urban lands every year. California, simply put, is not adequately addressing the use of PFAS.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: I would argue that many farmers are not told that they're even applying those PFAS chemicals, which could be very well contaminating their soil and their groundwater for generations. Prohibiting new PFAS in California will begin the slow reduction of this pollution from entering our bodies and our waterways and ultimately our food supply.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: And making PFAS pesticides restricted materials will provide pesticide users and the public more generally with more information regarding their use in California. Colleagues, I know that this bill is a work in progress. I also know that this is a tough vote.

statement: Well, good morning, senators. Thank you very much. I feel like this is an intimate conversation about a topic that I care deeply about. speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: And wanna go with, before we go any further, just mention that I will be accepting all of the committee amendments listed in comment eight of the committee analysis. As we all may know, California remains the center of the global film and television industry, but post production work, including editorial, sound scoring, visual effects, and finishing, is increasingly being performed in other jurisdictions that offer targeted competitive incentives. Current law limits eligibility for the California motion picture tax credit primarily to projects that complete principal photography in our state.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: As a result, post production work is often moved to competing jurisdictions that offer stand alone or more flexible incentives for post production activity. I hate to say it, but California's a little late to the game on this one.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: States and countries already offer and have offered for some time. These incentives include, but are not limited to the states of New York, New Jersey, as well as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. These policies have led to the migration of high wage jobs, vendor spending, and economic activity out of the state of California. Major post production editorial facilities, including scoring stages operated by Sony, Fox, Warner Brothers, and Skywalker Sound, are generating substantially less revenue than in previous years, and face the risk of closure.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: Economic analysis demonstrates that post production incentives generate significant returns on public investment through increased taxable wages, local vendor spending, and broader ancillary economic activity.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: Without a targeted post production incentive, California risks further losing a critical segment of the entertainment industry supply chain that has truly defined the state, even when creative leadership remains largely based in the state. AB 2319, if approved, would create the California Postproduction Tax Credit, a targeted incentive for qualified post production expenditures performed in California regardless of where principal photography occurred and subject to program requirements and oversight.

speaker: Nick Schultz
statement: I'd like to note that this post production tax credit is not tied to the $750 million budget for the Motion Picture Tax Credit that was passed last year. statement: This bill makes three targeted common sense fixes to the welfare exemption that together protect affordable housing, reduce administrative burden, and preserve housing stability for working families across California. speaker: Tiyesha Watts
statement: Under current law, if long term tenants and income rises modestly above the lower income threshold, up to a 140% of the area of medium income, their unit can still count toward the property's welfare exemption. speaker: Tiyesha Watts
statement: AB 2089 extends it one year to get the legislature and affordable housing advocates time to pursue a comprehensive unified solution. speaker: Tiyesha Watts
statement: Their practical result would be would be financial pressure on non profits to evict those tenants, the very outcome affordable housing is designed to prevent. We serve our immigrant and refugee communities in the Bay Area and Central Valley, and we are a proud cosponsor for AB 1633, which would impose a 50% tax on corporations operating private immigration detention centers.

speaker: Kimberly Wu
statement: I have loved ones who sought permanent residency for over twenty years, and when they got to their final interview, ICE agents handcuffed their hands and feet and forcefully shipped them to separate detention centers in California. Words cannot describe the pain of seeing your elder relative who immigrated to this country to build a better life for your family, to break down crying behind a glass screen window where it's impossible to hug them and hold their hand.

speaker: Kimberly Wu
statement: There are not enough words to comfort your loved one who are stripped from their personal belongings, their clothes, their medical needs, and their freedom. No one deserves to experience the pain, suffering, and loneliness that my loved ones felt every day in that prison. Private companies like Geo Group and Co Civic profit from caging people like my relatives who had never spent a single night apart in their decades long marriage until they were detained, fiances weeks away from their wedding, and young children separated from their mother.

speaker: Kimberly Wu
statement: I know these stories because they were in the room with me, waiting hours for a chance of a one hour visit for their loved ones. Private detention facilities hold thousands of people across California in inhumane conditions, like severe medical neglect, filthy water, rotting food and abuse, and poor access to legal representation.

speaker: Kimberly Wu
statement: The CEO of CoreCivic, one of the largest for profit pension corporations, reported $7,500,000 in annual compensation and more since then and noted that the recent rise in immigration sweeps was, quote, unquote, truly one of the most exciting periods in my career with the company. speaker: Kimberly Wu
statement: We respectfully urge your aye vote on AB 1633 to hold these corporations accountable and prioritize the safety and dignity of all Californians. Thank you.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: I'm proud to present AB 2084, which promotes continuity of services and prevents disruptions to California's nonprofit organizations. Recently, we've experienced a notable increase in federal scrutiny and rhetoric directed at our nonprofit organizations regarding their tax exempt status, creating a level of uncertainty that extends beyond established legal eligibility standards and raises serious concerns about stability and predictability. This creates risk for California based organizations that are otherwise fully compliant with federal and state law, but are caught up in shifting federal actions or narratives.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: California nonprofits, as we all know, provide vital services to our community members, and they rely on their status as a tax exempt organization to remain operable. Under current law, when federal status is stripped, the California Franchise Tax Board is required to revoke our state tax exempt status.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: Currently, the FTB does not have the authority to delay and review the action before nonprofits are hit with state revocation. This means the nonprofits providing essential services can lose state tax exempt status quickly through no fault of their own. This bill addresses that gap by giving the franchise tax board authority to use its discretion to maintain state income tax exempt status for 501c3 three organizations that sought original exemption through the streamlined 3500 a process.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: If federal revocation occurs for reasons not related to lead legal eligibility for revocation, This ensures that California nonprofits are protected from federal actions that may be influenced by the federal political landscape. It is narrowly crafted and does not expand eligibility or reduce oversight.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: It simply preserves status for organizations that are following the law. AB 2084 addresses a real and growing risk. It is necessary and timely to safeguard and ensure California retains control over its own standards and protects organization from consequences beyond their control. With me today in support is Jennifer Fearing, Sacramento advocate for the California Association of Nonprofits.

speaker: Timothy Grayson
statement: Two minutes, please.

speaker: Jennifer Fearing
statement: Thank you, Mister Chair. Jennifer Fearing, Sacramento advocate for California Association of Nonprofits. It's a 10,000 member organization, statewide policy alliance. Since 2008, nonprofits can pursue state tax exempt status expeditiously by filing the FTB's 3,500 a form that relies on the Federal Government's 501c3 determination.

speaker: Jennifer Fearing
statement: Almost a quarter of California's nonprofits have utilized this process. This reliance on the federal approval creates an efficiency, but also precarity. If the Federal Government revokes a nonprofit's, tax exempt status even for political reasons, the FTB is required to automatically revoke their state status as well. The FTB currently lacks that authority to delay or evaluate the merits of the actions for nonprofits that use the streamline process.

speaker: Jennifer Fearing
statement: Since federal threats began emerging in early 2025, Cal Nonprofits has continued to urge all 3,500 A nonprofits to initiate the longer form process to get independent validation from the state of their tax exempt status.

speaker: Jennifer Fearing
statement: And we are only here requesting this change in law because of specific and unprecedented federal threats and executive orders targeting nonprofits for their speech or mission driven work rather than any actual wrongdoing. speaker: Jennifer Fearing
statement: With their take tax exempt status in jeopardy, a nonprofit can find its grants and payments frozen, face new tax liabilities, and possibly have to reduce essential services to vulnerable people. It does not lower the bar for tax exemption.

speaker: Jennifer Fearing

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: Thank you very much, madam president. Members arise to present AB 2721 on behalf of Assemblymember Carrillo. This bill is a California Latino legislative caucus priority bill and is narrowly tailored, transparency measure intended to promote workplace safety and informed decision making for hospitality workers and hotel guests when federal immigration agencies are on hotel premises.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: The bill requires a hotel operator with actual knowledge of a reservation with the United States Customs and Border Protection or the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement to post a prominent notice in an accessible location where it can be seen by all workers. It provides a limited disclosure to hotel guests.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: Upon request of guests with a reservation, the hotel operator must disclose at the time of check-in the potential presence of CBP or ICE on the premises during the guest reservation. The bill does not require a physical notice to be provided to guests. The underlying issue is one of transparency and workplace safety. There is currently no statewide requirement that hotels disclose these reservations to hospitality workers.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: The absence of notice can create uncertainty for employees, limit informed decision making by guests, and potentially place workers in difficult or unsafe circumstances without adequate information about activities occurring in their workplace.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: When a hotel operator has actual knowledge of a covered reservation, the worker notice must be posted within forty eight hours. Importantly, this bill does not require a hotel operator to seek out or to independently obtain information regarding federal reservations. It only applies when they have actual knowledge. It does not prohibit hotels from hosting federal agencies, nor does it regulate or interfere with federal law enforcement operations.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: It does not prevent CBP or ICE from conducting lawful activities, including operations addressing drug trafficking, human trafficking, or other enforcement priorities.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: We already recognize in California law the importance of transparency, where information may materially affect consumers, and the importance of protecting workers from known hazards or unsafe situations. This bill applies those principles in a very narrow and specific context. This measure also contains a January 1, 2029 sunset clause, providing the legislature with an opportunity to evaluate implementation and determine whether any further action as required. Members of this bill has received bipartisan support. Respectfully ask for an aye vote.

speaker: Timothy Grayson
statement: Thank you, madam president. I am pleased to present AB 1383 by Assemblymember McKenner that will strengthen retirement security for our public employees by making three measured changes. First, this measure will adjust the pensionable compensation limit to align it with the current federal social security wage base by making a targeted increase to the pensionable compensation limit for those who don't participate in social security. This will help improve recruitment and retention for of all of our public employees.

speaker: Timothy Grayson
statement: Recent amendments reduce that limit used to calculate a defined benefit paid to a member who retires from a public employee retirement system from 135% to 120% of the federal Social Security limit for members whose service is not included in the federal system among minor technical adjustments.

speaker: Timothy Grayson
statement: Second, it lowers the normal retirement age for public safety employees from 57 to 55. This is critical because the international agency of for research on cancer has classified the occupation of a firefighter as a group one carcinogen. Reducing the normal retirement age to 55 will decrease exposures for firefighters and other public safety personnel.

speaker: Timothy Grayson
statement: And then finally, this measure will establish a new retirement formula for public safety, 3% of 55, and permit local agencies and their public safety employees to bargain over perspective increases within the allow allowable formulas. These formulas would be 2% at 55, 2.5% at 55, 2.7% at 55, or 3% at 55.

speaker: Timothy Grayson
statement: Employers and employees can bargain for a lower or higher formula that is closest to their current formula. Again, AB 1383 makes these targeted perspective make these only as targeted perspective, not retroactive or retrospective changes to our public employees' retirement policy in a manner that ensures that our retirement systems remain healthy and our public employees have a secure retirement. I am pleased that this measure has enjoyed bipartisan support.

speaker: Timothy Grayson
statement: And with the recent amendments, I invite my colleagues to join me in this effort, respectfully asking for an aye vote.

speaker: Angelique Ashby
statement: She's worked to craft the best policy while working with all stakeholders because this is a complex but critically important issue. The bill before you today takes a measured approach to closing a loophole in the Cartwright Act. California's Cartwright Act is our state's primary antitrust law, but it has an omission that AB 1776 seeks to fix. If two businesses conspire to undercut competition, that's illegal.

speaker: Angelique Ashby
statement: For the first time, under AB 1776, California will have a single firm conduct law on the books because we know that it doesn't take two businesses to act in an anti-competitive manner.

speaker: Angelique Ashby
statement: Federal law and 45 other states agree that one dominant company can be just as harmful as two companies acting together. This conversation is especially important now because consolidation has touched nearly every part of our economy. Since the 1990s, more than 75% of US industries have experienced increased market considerations. When companies gain that much power, it can mean higher prices, fewer choices, fewer opportunities for job creators to start small businesses, and suppressed wages for workers. We can see the impacts across every part of our state.

speaker: Angelique Ashby

speaker: Sabrina Cervantes
statement: Thank you, Madam President. I rise to present Assembly Bill 1881, the California Indian Freedom Act of 2026, on behalf of Assembly Member Ramos. The bill ensures that California Indians can freely practice their religious and spiritual traditions on state lands. California is home to the largest population of Native Americans in the United States, each with its own distinct culture and religion that has predated statehood, yet for centuries, there has been a longstanding policy in our country and in this state that has allowed for the suppression of tribal spirituality and cultural expression to assimilate the indigenous people by force.

speaker: Sabrina Cervantes
statement: California was home to 13 federal Indian boarding schools that abducted native children from their families, pushed them from speaking their languages, and prohibited their spiritual practices. These boarding schools resulted in generational trauma that continues to impact tribal communities to this date. Unfortunately, the legacy of Indian assimilation and cultural suppression still shapes present day policy. Sacred sites are still desecrated, developed, and made inaccessible. Many tribes remain separated from cultural items and their ancestors' remains often held by universities and museums.

speaker: Sabrina Cervantes
statement: Tribal members are routinely questioned or harassed for carrying ceremonial items in public spaces. Native students and their families still face obstacles on prohibitions on wearing regalia at graduation ceremonies despite federal and state statutory protections. These are not isolated incidents, but the direct result of state and federal policies that sought to erase native identity from our country. The bill aims to afford Native Americans the same level of protection for their faith as we do for other religions.

speaker: Sabrina Cervantes
statement: For many tribal communities, their faith depend on access to sacred sites to gather traditional plants and foods and enjoy the freedom to use their ceremonial items without being questioned every step of the way. 1881 establishes clear, enforceable standards. No state agency may substantially burden a California tribe's right to religious practice unless the state can demonstrate a compelling interest in doing so.

speaker: Sabrina Cervantes
statement: Even then, it must do so by the least restrictive means possible. State agencies are to allow access to sacred sites on state lands and permit gathering of traditional plants, foods, and other materials essential to tribal religious practices. The bill further protects the handling of sacred items and regalia on state grounds, including here at the State Capitol.

speaker: Sabrina Cervantes
statement: I wanna note that floor amendments that the author took, which made clarification, including that tribes should have exclusive standing to enforce one of the provisions of the bill. This bill is about safeguarding California's first people's religious freedoms, not only as a human right, but as a matter of cultural survival. I respectfully ask for an aye vote on AB 1881.

speaker: John Laird
statement: Thank you very much, Madam President. SB 577 is back for concurrence. This bill deals with childhood sexual assault and has been the subject of much discussion since the bill left this house over a year ago. Normally, in concurring with Assembly amendments, the debate focuses solely on the amendments taken in the Assembly. In this case, the totality of the bill, along with these amendments, is important to discuss.

speaker: John Laird
statement: The adoption of AB 218 in 2019, which extended the statute of limitations on child sexual assault cases with public entities, brought forward heartbreaking cases of mistreatment of young Californians while in the care of public agencies and provided a path for justice. Unfortunately, other issues also arose from AB 2181, one major issue being the financial ability of public agencies to respond.

speaker: John Laird
statement: Two years ago, a study of this issue was authorized by the Legislature and was conducted by the Fiscal Crisis and Management Assistance Team, FCMAT. As then the Chair of Budget Sub 1 on Education, I held a hearing on this matter. It showed that insurance premiums for schools had jumped an estimated 700% over the past decade, and schools are paying for retroactive claims for abuse that occurred when they were part of a joint powers agreement, even if they are no longer part of that joint powers agreement.

speaker: John Laird
statement: Local governments are declaring fiscal emergencies, and various recommendations from FCMAT were actually what started the Senate Bill 577.

speaker: John Laird
statement: As a result, SB 577 provides various financing mechanisms to public entities such as bonding, judicial review of award amounts in old cases, and ability to opt in for longer payment periods. SB 577 also provides avenues for local agencies to respond to mounting liability from childhood sexual assault claims, while ensuring that survivors maintain meaningful, accessible pathways to justice.

speaker: John Laird
statement: The bill includes important fraud prevention that will penalize attorneys that bring forth bad faith or fraudulent cases and ensure required documentation is required with the cases. This bill also enables public entities to better defend against very old cases where witnesses or records no longer exist. Importantly, the bill also includes significant prevention measures to ensure children in schools, juvenile detention facilities, foster care facilities, and more will be protected from future abuse.

speaker: John Laird
statement: Additionally, an amendment was added in the Assembly regarding public agency tort liability. If a district's liability is determined to be 15% or under, the financial liability is subject to that similar limit to not exceed 15%. But let me be clear, this body does not support turning a blind eye to abuse occurring in institutions that owed a duty of care to these children. That is why Senate Bill 577 includes important prevention and accountability measures.

speaker: John Laird
statement: Senate Bill 577 does not shut the door to justice. There are no cutoffs to claims. There are no caps. When I successfully got this bill out of the Assembly Judiciary Committee last year, there was opposition from a school organization saying the bill did not go far enough. There was opposition from a survivor's group saying the bill went too far.

speaker: John Laird
statement: That same dynamic is in play right now with this bill. It is an indicator that we have strived to maintain balance. There is opposition from law enforcement organizations, and let me speak to that for a second, regarding the addition of the Office of Youth and Community Restoration to the list of entities that can access personnel records. Existing law includes strict confidentiality for any authorized entities accessing personnel records.

speaker: John Laird

This bill, the California Learner Personal Information Protection Act, makes critical improvements to California's student data privacy laws to reflect the modern reality of our education system and protect students.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: The Student Online Personal Information Protection Act was signed was signed into law in 2014 to combat the risks associated with the use of technology in the classroom. Since that time, as we all know, educational technology has evolved dramatically.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: When a student answers questions and required courseware becomes part of their digital educational record. Some companies even get student information from data brokers. All of this comes together to create profiles that extend well beyond the information knowingly provided by students.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: AB 1159 will ensure that information collected from any California student for educational purposes is used only for educational purposes and cannot be misused. First, it builds on existing student data privacy laws clarifying and expanding their protections and modernizing them to account for new threats to student privacy.

speaker: Steve Padilla
statement: Second, it extends the same protections to higher education students. And third, creates meaningful enforcement, including a limited private right of action, modeled after the student borrower bill of rights for students harmed by violation.

speaker: Steve Padilla

speaker: Sade Elhawary
statement: Thank you so much, Mister speaker and members. This bill is really about transparency, about data, about continuing to keep our children safe by adding to existing reporting requirements. Today, there was a LA Times story that specifically tackles this issue and the need for more data. I respectfully ask for your aye vote and want to make sure that everyone is clear that this will not touch, and will not repeal any existing policies around time, place, and matter. Thank you.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you, Assemblymember El Hawari. Assemblymember Gabriel, you are recognized.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: Yeah. Thank you very much, Mister speaker. I rise to offer some thoughts on this bill. And I know many of you have reached out to ask if the Jewish caucus has a position on the bill, and the answer is that we do not as a caucus. The caucus is not asking you to vote against the bill.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: I'm not asking you to vote against the bill. I know that there have been significant amendments that have taken to remove opposition from Jewish California. But I did wanna just take a moment to have a conversation about the broader topic here so that folks could understand the genesis of the bill that, a Senate bill, that twelve eighty seven that was a Jewish caucus party bill, that this bill originally sought to repeal.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: And that was a bill that, was, introduced by the caucus after some very specific incidents. And let me say at the beginning, I believe very, very deeply in the freedom of speech and the right to protest.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: I grew up in a family where my with activist parents. I went to many protests and rallies and marches as a kid. I believe deeply in the right of protest for social justice, and I also believe in the right of free speech. And I think that that means, especially, young people on our college campuses have the right to criticize, our government, the government of Israel, China, Russia, Ukraine, Gavin Newsom, Jesse Gabriel, everybody in between. And that is a sacred right.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: And I also believe that we, in many ways, have lost the ability as a society to hear opinions that we that are different from our own. And that has been a message that I've delivered to my own community. All of us need to be willing to listen to opinions that are different from our own.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: And and I actually was thinking about as I have listened to some of the beautiful comments from our colleagues who are terming out, one of the most powerful experiences for me in this body has been to hear and learn from people whose life experiences are so different from my own. That has been an enormous life gift and I will be forever grateful for it.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: But thiS Bill that the Jewish caucus introduced as SB 1287 was, introduced after a very specific incident at UC Berkeley in which a group of Jewish students hosted an event and a group of students with a different perspective put out a call to shut it down. And so they came as protesters. The event was moved for purposes of security. They came as protesters. They overwhelmed the event.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: They broke windows at Zellerbach Hall. A number of students were physically injured. A constituent of mine, Brooke Resnick, was choked and ended up having to seek medical care. And for from our perspective, that's not that's not free speech. And so we introduced a bill AB 1287.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: I wanna let you know what it does. It says that there has that universities have to have clear, content neutral time, place, and manner restrictions so everybody, irrespective of their viewpoint, gets to express their viewpoint. That those policies have to prohibit the following things, violence, harassment, intimidation, and discrimination, and that they have to be published so every student understands them. That was the essence of that bill. And we went through Mister Calra's committee.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: We worked very hard with him and his staff to make sure that there were robust first amendment protections, and it passed off this floor by a vote of 70 to zero. Because we believe that everybody deserves the right to be heard, and everybody deserves the right to protest, but everybody also deserves the right to be free from violence and free from harassment.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: And so it was very concerning to our caucus, to see an effort without a conversation to repeal that bill, To take away those time, place, and manner restrictions. And I would submit to all of you that time, place, and manner restrictions actually support free speech. They are supportive because it means that even you can't go shut down another group of students because you disagree with them.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: And so while I will get up and defend the right of student protesters to say whatever they want, no matter how much I disagree with it, I will always always believe that all of our students must be able to gather together and not be subject to physical violence. No student should end up having to seek medical care because they were wanted to bring a speaker to campus. And so, I just wanna mark this moment. I'm not asking anybody to vote against this bill.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: This bill has been significantly amended, but I worry that the intent the effort of this bill is to begin a process that will ultimately result in the, repealing of civil rights protections.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: And I think that there should be a very high bar for that, particularly when they're passed in this environment by such a strong and overwhelming vote. And so I just wanna say, understanding how this bill started and where it's been moved to, if there's an effort a year from now, two years from now, three years from now to undo those hard wrought civil rights protections, I just wanted to mark this moment.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: Because, again, I believe very deeply in the right to protest, Very deeply in the right to free speech. All of us should protect that right, irrespective of what the speaker is saying, especially on our college campuses. And we have to do better.

speaker: Jesse Gabriel
statement: All of us have to do better about making sure that young people are exposed to ideas that they disagree with and are different from their own. But at the same time, we have to make sure that that protest does not involve silencing other people. And at a minimum, does not involve other people being subject to violence, harassment, intimidation, and discrimination. And that is a line that I believe that we need to hold. And for that reason, I wanted to share those thoughts, Mister speaker.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you, Assemblymember Gabriel. Assemblymember Brian, you are recognized.

speaker: Isaac Bryan
statement: I wanna thank my colleague from South Central and my colleague, Fermincino, the Chair of our Jewish caucus, vice Chair of the Black Caucus. The Black Caucus has also been asked often what our position is on this bill, and the caucus as a whole does not have a formal position on this bill.

speaker: Isaac Bryan
statement: And similar to my colleague from Encino, I too just wanna mark this moment because I think our colleague from South Central is doing the foundation of what all good policy should be, which is rooted in data and evidence. And I remember 1287 because I sat on that judiciary committee, and I did not vote for it. And I didn't vote for it on this floor.

speaker: Isaac Bryan
statement: Because of the same concerns that our colleague just raised, I was concerned we were going down a very slippery slope with civil rights and protesting. One that I don't know has been born out by that bill in the same way that the inverse hasn't been shown. It's why we need data.

speaker: Isaac Bryan
statement: We need to understand how best to protect the learning spaces of our young people so that competing ideas and challenging thoughts about this complicated world that we all coexist in can arise in a safe and healthy way, in the appropriate ways, at the appropriate times. Also, understanding that the appropriate time, place, and manner often comes from the young people who are creating those protests.

speaker: Isaac Bryan
statement: I came directly from a college campus to this body. I still often find myself in protests in the streets of Los Angeles, and y'all know this. But I wanna thank my colleague from South Central because standing for what you believe is right even when it seems difficult is hard. Having the necessary conversations you need to have to remove opposition and bring folks to the table around shared goals is hard and at times feels impossible.

speaker: Isaac Bryan
statement: And the work that has been done to get this data centered bill to this point is commendable.

speaker: Isaac Bryan
statement: And it has my support today, and I also will not be asking anyone not to vote for it. I think you probably should vote for it.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you. Assemblymember Brian. Mister Lee, I had you down. Okay. Assemblymember Garcia, you are recognized.

speaker: Robert Garcia
statement: Thank you, Mister speaker. And members, I rise in strong support of AB 2551, a bill which ensures students are not threatened by simply exercising their freedom of speech. And before I continue, I just really wanna say, thank you to Mister speaker Rivas for just allowing this bill to be heard because I know that is sometimes difficult.

speaker: Robert Garcia
statement: As an educator, I strongly believe that education is meant to uplift students, and campuses should always serve as a safe space for students to practice their civic engagement and participate in our democracy. Student activism has always been a powerful tool for progress, and this bill is a simple study bill to ensure that there is an application of justice towards students that is fair and free from discrimination or harassment.

speaker: Robert Garcia
statement: In the spring of twenty twenty four, around 500 students were disciplined and arrested for participating in protests, and students have expressed that the enforcement of this discipline has been inequitable. AB 2551 will provide us with data. As my colleague from Los Angeles stated, just data. It's not a retreat, it's data to allow us to determine if these responses were indeed inequitable.

speaker: Robert Garcia
statement: Thousands of students from my district attend Cal State San Bernardino and UC Riverside, and we all have students in our district aspiring to do their part to change the world.

speaker: Robert Garcia
statement: They deserve to know that speaking up for what they believe in will not jeopardize their education. Our public university's values lie in being open to diverse perspectives, setting high ethical standards, leading by example, and advancing positive change in California, the nation, and beyond. So when California students are empowered by these values, they should never feel unsafe on the campuses, which many of them call their second home.

speaker: Robert Garcia
statement: I want to deeply thank the author from Los Angeles for bringing this forward, this important measure, and I do respectfully ask for your aye vote.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you, Assemblymember Garcia. Assemblymember Bauer Kehund, you are recognized.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: Thank you, Mister speaker and members. I rise in a similar posture as my colleague from the San Fernando Valley. I agree this is a data bill, and I'm not asking you to not vote for it. But I I felt compelled to stand up and speak because many of you weren't here when we went through what led to the bill that is the subject of this data. And we all, many of us, bring trauma to this floor.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: And I acknowledge my own, so so I just wanna say that. You know, I was raised by a grandmother who was kicked out of school because she was Jewish. So the way Jews are treated on campus is something that is critically important to me personally. And to watch what happened at UCLA where they've set up blockades and Jewish students were blocked from attending class unless they said certain things is not free speech. It is the opposite.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: It is forced speech. And the campus let that happen for days and days. Kids were locked in buildings. They were blocked from attending their classes. These were students who'd pay a lot of money to attend our UCs and just wanted an education.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: And as much as one should be able to choose to be a part of a protest, one should be able to choose not to be part of a protest. That is the freedom guaranteed under our constitution, and that was not happening at UCLA. And so we saw a failure on our campuses to allow for free speech in a way that protected students, protected students physically as my colleague from the San Fernando Valley said, but also protected students' rights to differing opinions. And that was painful.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: It was it hurt to see Jewish students treated that way across California on our own campuses.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: And so Senator Glazer took on this effort. It wasn't an easy one as was mentioned by my colleague from LA. He was here. But it was one that we succeeded in because of collaboration and conversation and a shared commitment to allowing for protest in a way that did not harm other people on campus. And from where I sit, I have seen that we have changed the dynamic at least at my local UC.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: I mostly have experience at Berkeley because that's where I am in the state. But we have seen just at the beginning of the year last year, students tried to block, say, their gate and stop students from getting onto campus in a protest. And the university said, no. You cannot block access to classes. Right?

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: That is not following our time, place, and manner restrictions. And they had to remove the blockade. They were allowed to speak in the time, place, and manner that's allowed, but they were not allowed to block other students. To me, that is our time, place, and manner restrictions working.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: And so I just had to get up and say that it is critically important that we allow for free speech, but we also have to acknowledge the pain and hurt and exclusion that was happening on our campuses at the time, and that will absolutely continue to happen if we roll back the protections that we are succeeding in allowing for debate, for conversation, for protest, but also preventing the harm to many, many students.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: Frankly, I didn't really know what I was gonna do on this bill. I'm not gonna support it, but and that is merely because of the numbers. I'm worried that the data we're talking about here, there's so few students. So just last year, of 300,000 students on our UCs, there were 71 time, place, and manner violations. And on our CSUs, out of 460,000 students, there were 200.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: So I also just want us to be conscious as we move forward and get this data to put it into context. I don't know what the data will show, but as any good social scientist knows, you need a good sample size to have meaningful data. And so what what those numbers tell me is we're not overly restricting speech, but we also need to be careful not to roll back civil rights violations because we have a small data set.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: And the small data set frankly shows that we aren't being too restrictive as far as I'm concerned. So I just wanted to harness in this moment the importance of the work that I believe we have done together.

speaker: Rebecca Bauer-Kahan
statement: At a vote of 70 to zero, I think that this was a collaboration across parties, across ideal logical barriers to make sure that our campuses allow for free speech and protect our students. And I'm proud of that work, and I hope that we stand together in the future to continue to protect it.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you. Assemblymember Bauer Kehinde. Doctor Jackson, you are recognized.

speaker: Corey Jackson
statement: Thank you very much, Mister speaker. You know, I ever since a few years ago when we all ended up on the menu at the same time, it became evident that we lost our ability to be in solidarity with one another in a genuine way. And I became very concerned when I saw people who I even consider my allies in my district begin to lose their own humanity as they profess to protect other people's humanity.

speaker: Corey Jackson
statement: And at the end of the day, it became evident that we were all losing. The bill for the Jewish caucus that went through higher education, I did vote on it.

speaker: Corey Jackson
statement: And I voted on it for a particular reason. And that is you cannot step on the back of one group in order to fight for another group. It is wrong. And you are becoming the devil in which you profess to be fighting against. And so what we have to do is we have to center humanity and understand there are universal humanistic principles that we have to be guided by.

speaker: Corey Jackson
statement: And it can't be guided by who has greater humanity over another. Now I'll be voting on this bill for one simple reason, because we have to also make sure that institutions are not weaponizing this that goes beyond what the true intent was, and I don't think anyone wants to see that happen. I'm a college professor, a college president, or someone, and I don't like this particular group or what they're saying, so now I am going to punish them because I don't agree with a particular message.

speaker: Corey Jackson
statement: But one thing that I'm also concerned with is that we are still trying to choose one group after another, and we've got a lot more work to be doing on this. And I believe next year, especially those who are leaders of ethnic caucuses, need to come together in a real way.

speaker: Corey Jackson
statement: And to sit down in an authentic humanistic way to really work through how to be in true solidarity with one another just as human beings. Because for some reason, on a whole host of bills over the last two years, we've done just enough, but we know we haven't gone all the way the way we need to and the way our ancestors have been able to do before us.

speaker: Corey Jackson
statement: So our hope that as we go into next year, because next year, those of us who continues to be on the menu will be intensified as we go into the next presidential election, and we know how this cycle is. We're gonna have to do some deep, deep work, and we have to work on our souls. And we have to bring our allies also to the table with us because they have some work to be done on these issues.

speaker: Corey Jackson
statement: Because if we can't get it right now, the next generations will have no clue how to work through this in the future. Let that be our charge. Let that be our calling for next year as we do better to heal and work on our souls together. I respectfully ask for an aye vote.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you, doctor Jackson. Assembly member Muratsuchi, you are recognized.

speaker: Al Muratsuchi
statement: Thank you very much. I I just want to rise to acknowledge and express my appreciation to the comments from the Chair of the Jewish caucus. You know, I I know that this has been a extremely sensitive debate in this house and that I was a part of that those conversations.

speaker: Al Muratsuchi
statement: But I I wanna take this opportunity to make it absolutely clear that, you know, while we strive to make policies that truly foster, the spirit and the atmosphere of of free speech for all, that we wanna make sure that there is absolutely no place for students to be assaulted, for, you know, minorities, whether religious or otherwise, to be felt targeted, where they don't feel safe in going to school, to be at school, to go to class.

speaker: Al Muratsuchi
statement: And so, you know, whether it's the proponents of this bill or anyone else, we we need to start with those basic ground rules that, yes, we all want to support free speech, but we all want to make sure that every student, every child, it feels safe and supported.

speaker: Al Muratsuchi
statement: And so I just want to take that opportunity to make my position absolutely clear.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you. Assembly member Muratsuchi. Assembly member Lee, you are recognized.

speaker: Alex Lee
statement: Thank you, Mister speaker. I rise in strong support of AB 2551. Members, I just wanna center us onto the soul of this bill is about protecting our students. Now the only other elected office I held before this one, I was a student body president at UC Davis. And you can bet you at UC Davis, we had a lot of problems and protests with tuition thawing, Un thawing, chancellors coming, going, presidents coming, going, different wars and things happening, and things did get ugly.

speaker: Alex Lee
statement: And students did get emotionally and sometimes physically hurt, and that was very troubling. But when something I wanna uplift to what our colleague from Moreno Valley talked about is what we all say in United is in two things. Making sure that our students are bodily and mentally safe, and secondly, preventing those same institutions which often can have their own biases and leadership egos from weaponizing these policies meant to keep students safe to using those policies that weaponize against students.

speaker: Alex Lee
statement: And we don't want those things to happen too. I think I commend a lot of the author to boil down the bill today to basically about data transparency.

speaker: Alex Lee
statement: And really importantly, also we haven't discussed is compelling and open forum. Now when I was president, more often than not, students of all political persuasion were united by one thing, that the administration sucks. They would not listen to us and they felt that if we weren't given a real process to address our grievances, you'd have to lash out. Now doctor Martin Luther King said, a riot is the language of the is the voice of those who would go unheard. And that happens even on our campuses.

speaker: Alex Lee
statement: Right? We wanna make sure that our students are empowered through the legal and right methods to actually get their grievances addressed, and not just in a performative way. And not just a performative way where they wait for you to graduate or leave, but you want them to actually meaningfully participate in the shared model, at least in the UCE system, especially they talk about is the shared governance model. Right? And the students are part of that.

speaker: Alex Lee
statement: And so I really appreciate the debate today about how we need to protect the civil rights of all students. But also, I don't think it is the intention of the author to roll back any civil rights or undo work that has been done in the past. I think this is an important student protection at the heart of it, and we wanna make sure that students of all political persuasions can express themselves freely and safely.

speaker: Alex Lee
statement: And we don't want it to get to the part where people are smashing windows or hurting other people because we want people to feel that the legal avenues of expressing their their their views are actually valid and actually have meaning. But when those avenues are closed, that's when people get agitated, they get angry, and get frustrated, and we don't want that at the same time.

speaker: Alex Lee
statement: And we have certainly don't want and I've, you know, I've had some of this experience too, administrators and chancellors who have their own agendas to police certain students because they don't like them just like our colleague from Reno Valley talked about. So I really appreciate the debate today, a very thoughtful, robust conversation that has also led to the amendments that have come up today. And I respectfully ask for a strong I vote on AB 2551.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you. Assemblymember Lee, assemblymember's board, you are recognized.

speaker: Tasha Boerner
statement: Mister speaker, members, I wanted to make a couple comments because I'm not gonna be able to support the bill today. And it's not because I don't believe in robust free speech and protest rights for students on campus. But I represented UCLA and did so two years ago when the student protests were happening on campus and saw really horrific things happening to Jewish students. There were portions of the campus that were blocked from them.

speaker: Tasha Boerner
statement: My staff could not enter portions of the campus unless they made statements that were in conflict with their Jewish identity and their Jewish principles.

speaker: Tasha Boerner
statement: My staff saw Jewish students being beaten with campus police ten and twenty feet away by protesters while the university did nothing to address it. And so I appreciate that the author has turned this into more of a study and a data bill.

speaker: Tasha Boerner
statement: But the thing that many of my constituents are worried about is that this is leading to and intentionally leading to time, place, and manner restrictions that the University of California has put in place that has resulted in their protection and protection that has been really needed and necessary. So I know that that is not the author's intent on this, but there is a significant concern in my community that the that this process could lead to to to removal of important protections.

speaker: Tasha Boerner
statement: We do need to have make sure that those protections allow for robust free speech, robust protest.

speaker: Tasha Boerner
statement: But we also have to make sure, I think, as my colleague from Torrance said, that it that exclusion from activities, beating, harassment, those kinds of things are not part of free speech. And so I know the University of California is against this bill, I think, because they believe that they got this right. I Aye, I do, think that I've I've met with them and looked at their time, place, and manner restrictions down in UCLA, and I do think that they've gotten this to a good place.

speaker: Tasha Boerner
statement: So because of that and because of, I think, the concern that this is would lead to weakening civil rights protections and time, place, and manage restrictions that will actually protect all students. I'm gonna need to not support the bill today, but I wanna thank you today.

speaker: Tasha Boerner
statement: Thanks.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you Assemblymember Spohr. Assemblymember Bonta, you are recognized.

speaker: Mia Bonta
statement: Thank you. I rise in support of AB 2551, and I wanna commend our colleague from South Los Angeles for bringing this forward. I think one of the most important things that we are required to do as legislators is to understand what happens when we pass the measure and the the the implications of that in implementation.

speaker: Mia Bonta
statement: I'm certain I was a part of that 70 to zero vote that ensured that we could protect our Jewish students, our students on campus, when the first bill was brought forward. And I'm also just as clear that sometimes in implementation, people get impacted in a way that we do not intend.

speaker: Mia Bonta
statement: If there are 271 students that have been called to be in violation of this measure, that's 271 students who perhaps as the Assembly member has shared, have been put on probation for not being and not able to continue on in their education. Those are people who have fought to be able to make sure that they could get onto campus in the first place, and then may be struggling with being able to stay on that campus for doing the simple thing of using their voice.

speaker: Mia Bonta
statement: And my daughter sits on a CSU campus. She talked to me about having the feeling of having her voice stifled because of the policies of the university. I want us to be clear about what this bill is seeking to do.

speaker: Mia Bonta
statement: Crystal clear. One is to hold public forums on selected campuses to elicit student feedback regarding the institution's time, place, and manner policies. And second, to provide, data on student code of conduct violations that occurred during or as a result of protest on campus.

speaker: Mia Bonta
statement: I think as legislators, we have to be able to create the space to be able to examine the implementation and the impact of the policies that move forward so that we don't have any student feeling like they are risking being able to continue on with their education because an individual campus may or may not have gotten this right. And this bill is very plainly trying to ensure that student students on their campuses have the ability to have a conversation with their administration.

speaker: Mia Bonta
statement: And that is very powerful. So I will be certainly supporting this bill on this and recognize certainly the concerns of those who have spoken on this floor as well. I do not believe that having conversations and asking administrations to hold forums to bring their students together does anything but strengthen the democratic process, strengthen their ability to participate fully in their academic settings, and ensure that we have a possibility to make sure that when we pass legislation on this floor that our institutions get it right.

speaker: Mia Bonta
statement: I respectfully request your aye vote.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you. Assembly member Bonta. Assembly member Bennett, you are recognized.

speaker: Steve Bennett
statement: Thank you, Mister speaker. Members, I rise with great humility that I have anything to offer to this debate. But I feel compelled to say this, and that is I believe that I represent a number of us who look to our ethnic caucuses for insights and for leadership. And so I would very much like to echo the comments of my colleague from the Moreno Valley that the efforts to try to work together is so valuable for this body and for the state of California.

speaker: Steve Bennett
statement: And quite frankly, today, I'm so impressed by how professional and how appropriate everybody with strong views is handling themselves here.

speaker: Steve Bennett
statement: California is in good shape with this kind of leadership. And I offer great grace to our ethnic caucuses as they continue. There is going to be no one effort that's going to solve this issue. It's going to be continuing efforts. It is a work in progress, and my compliments to everybody.

speaker: Steve Bennett
statement: Thank you very much.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you. Assemblymember Bennett. Assemblymember Berman, you are recognized.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: Thank you, Mister speaker. And I I rise in the spirit of my colleagues from the San Fernando Valley and from Orinda, and not not trying to discourage anybody from voting for this bill.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: And I know some of you know that my my dad is from South Africa, but I haven't talked at at all, I don't think, about how he and his older brothers were very, very involved in in an organization called NUSAS, the the National Union of South African Students that led the fight against apartheid in South Africa that brought Robert Kennedy, then Senator Kennedy to South Africa for his Ripple of Hope speech that he gave, which which ended up being one of his most famous speeches that he gave.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: And and my dad and my uncles, his older brothers all had to leave South Africa after they graduated from college. And they were lucky that they had the opportunity to leave South Africa, which a lot of others didn't, because of their anti apartheid activism when they were young.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: So I agree with pretty much everybody on this floor that I've heard speak and strong, strong support for the freedom of speech and for the right of students on our campuses to protest, when they think that there's there's a wrong either on campus or a wrong in the world. I've also been heartened to hear, from colleagues like my colleague from San Jose, the importance of making sure that our campuses are safe places physically and intellectually and emotionally for every student. For every student.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: And we'd failed that. We'd failed that, on our campuses in California.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: And that's what led to the legislation that was passed by Senator Glazer a couple of years ago. And we've also, you know, very accurately noted that this bill is a a study bill. It's a bill to collect data. I think some of us have a little apprehension because that is not how the bill started. The bill started as an attempt to roll back the civil rights protections that, we we passed into law a couple of years ago.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: And so that's why you hear some anxiety, from myself, and that's why you hear, some anxiety from some colleagues is because there's a concern that that is the goal of this effort, and and something that that we would not be able to support.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: And so the one thing I would ask, the author, my my colleague and friend from Los Angeles, is is for commitment to the to the, you know, very powerful points of my colleague from Moreno Valley that we all work together on this in the future. And that there's dialogue at the beginning of the process, which did not happen this time.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: And and that, you know, instead of some groups feeling like they get blindsided by an effort, that that that rather everybody gets a opportunity to participate in it. And so, would would ask my colleague to speak to that in in their close.

speaker: Marc Berman
statement: Thank you very much, Mister speaker.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Thank you, Assemblymember Berman. Assemblymember Rodriguez, you are recognized.

speaker: Celeste Rodriguez
statement: Thank you, Mister speaker. We don't often get opportunities like this to discuss, challenging matters, and I'm I'm also very grateful that we do have this opportunity. I want to, just recognize, what we heard in the higher education committee when we evaluated this bill. And it was a young woman who lost the opportunity to graduate because of a technical piece put into place by her university. It had nothing to do with the matters we've been discussing today.

speaker: Celeste Rodriguez
statement: It was some sort of labor dispute, and she wanted to be able to lift her voice for what she believed in, which we're all saying we agree that students should be able to lift their voice. statement: Thank you, madam speaker. Good afternoon, members. I rise on behalf of Senator Capaldi to, present SB 960.
