Currently, a community college can only offer a bachelor's degree if no campus of the CSU or the UC offers a similar program.

speaker: David Alvarez
statement: This has led to years of contentious debate over duplication, often stalling programs and denying students the access to degrees they need for their local jobs. statement: Thank you, madam speaker. Members, AB 179 is back for concurrence. Last time we voted, this body voted on AB 179 to pass the Assembly floor with unanimous bipartisan support. It also passed the Senate, 39 to zero unanimous bipartisan support. I believe that the vote reflects something that we are hearing loud and clear from the people of California.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: They're demanding that we act. Parents are asking us to step up and protect their children from the harmful design choices built into today's social media platforms. And as legislators, we have a responsibility to listen and respond. I'd like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who's helped work on this bill, the many stakeholders, especially the bipartisan group of joint authors, co authors, and most importantly, the staff who have invested countless hours and weekends into getting AB 179 to where it is today.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: I'm very proud of the collaborative spirit that we have taken to getting this bill to where it is.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: This bill would not be where it is today without their hard work, and I wanna recognize especially, the staff of Assembly privacy and judiciary committees, Senate privacy and judiciary committees, legislative counsel, the attorney general's office, and the governor's office. Incredibly grateful for the time and expertise that has been put into this bill. The bill was amended in the Senate to take a more targeted approach.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: Rather than imposing a blanketed age restriction that would have prohibited kids 16 from using social media platforms with addictive features, the bill now requires platforms to ensure that users 16 are just not provided with addictive features. This means that kids 16 could still use Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, and other covered social media platforms, but the platform must disable addictive features for those accounts.

speaker: Josh Lowenthal
statement: In other words, the bill regulates how the platforms are designed for kids, not whether kids can access social media altogether. Proud of the work that has been put into this bill has moved throughout the process, and I feel now this bill addresses what we were truly trying to address all along, prohibiting children from the most harmful and addictive design practices these platforms use. The Assembly stood together on this issue once before, respectfully ask you to do so again.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: Thank you so much, Madam Speaker and members. As many of you know, I have been starting to get a nickname up here in Sacramento as Chiquita Pilar because I talk about Chiquita Canyon Landfill in my community so much. And this bill is really trying to make sure that we don't have the kind of tragedy that we have in our community happening. So, for those who are unaware, we have a burning landfill, Chiquita Canyon Landfill, in our community.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: I heard about it and actually went and slept at a neighbor's house to experience it myself and had, within a half hour a headache.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: I had burning eyes and skin, and many of the symptoms that I've heard from so many people in my community. And since then, we have been fighting for a health study. We have been fighting for help to keep our community safe from the toxic air. And AB 28, the Landfill Safety Act, is back on concurrence after delaying for a year because of the process going through the California Air Resources Board to, regulate landfill methane to create a landfill methane regulation.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: Our community was involved in making that one of the strongest in the nation, if not the strongest.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: And this bill is really about prevention. Preventing the kind of tragedy that we have seen in our community where community members have come up for all of the hearings that we have done here to share their heartbreaking stories. Jose talked about the tremors that he has. He can no longer cook. He had a restaurant.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: He lost his restaurant and lost his home. Darcy and his family had to leave their house in the middle of the night because they could not breathe and go sleep in their car at the Walmart parking lot. Brandy and Steven had to sell their home. Brandy is fighting cancer and actually showed up to a recent press conference that we did with her bag of chemotherapy because it was too hot to leave it in the car.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: And she's also suffered five different miscarriages, which is common in our community.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: Darcy, who slept in the Walmart parking lot, could look at every single one of his neighbors, and they all have cancer. And just in the last few weeks, they've heard of a handful of people in the same community who had to have heart surgeries. We have so, so many people, Elizabeth, who many days cannot even get out of bed. People are disabled in our community because they're being made so sick by the toxic air.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: If you think about, especially on a day like today, all of the trash that we are throwing away, if that were to be burning.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: And many of you came and saw it and experienced it and had headaches yourselves by just being for a short time in our community. It is plastic that is burning. It is 90 acres of trash that is burning over 260 degrees. That's hotter than boiling water. And there is so much toxic liquid in the landfill that now the slope and the hillside is becoming unstable and having to get buttressed.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: This is costing millions of dollars a month. Our state cannot afford it. Our community's health cannot afford it. And AB 28 is saying and built on a foundation set by the EPA saying you should not get above a 131 degrees. Long-standing standard.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: And that if you do, you simply have to come up with a plan to fix it and get that temperature back down. Methane out of the, the system. But, unfortunately, there's been a culture in our landfill operators to hot-rod landfills. One of I have three landfills. I am blessed.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: Three landfills in my district. And one of the other landfill operators said that they didn't really work until it got to a 150 degrees. We have to make sure that they're taking action earlier. It saves lives, and it saves money for our state.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: I wanna thank our staff who has worked so, so hard, both past staff and current staff, our staff in the district, and our community who has been a canary in the coal mine on this issue and making a difference for the rest of the state.

speaker: Pilar Schiavo
statement: We have three landfills on fire right now, 11 with waivers to operate at a higher temperature, and we cannot afford this. So please, take this seriously if it's happening in your community. And with that, I respectfully request an aye vote.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: Thank you, Madam Chair and members. I rise to present SB 1203, which is the Stand for Security Act on behalf of Senator Smallwood-Cuevas. Security offers—officers—are an essential workforce. Every day, they protect our hospitals, our transit systems, our stores, our workplaces, our businesses, and our public buildings. There are over 300,000 security officers in California.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: They're often the first people called when something goes wrong, when someone is angry, distressed, or in crisis. We ask them to walk into difficult and unpredictable situations, sometimes with only seconds to make a decision that can affect people's lives.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: I see this every day in San Francisco where I live, where if you walk around our streets and you see people who are suffering with addiction or mental illness, who are in need, who are homeless, who may be engaged in criminal behavior, it's often the security officers that are the first to respond. But, unfortunately, I haven't always made the same investment in preparing and protecting them that we expect them to make in protecting us.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: When we don't properly prepare security officers, everyone is put at greater risk—the officer, the person in crisis, and the public. That's why SB 1203 is so important.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: It does a few simple things to help to prepare these security officers and essential workforce to safely and professionally do their jobs. It requires eight additional hours of in-person deescalation training, giving officers more tools to resolve dangerous situations before they become violent.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: It ensures that required training is paid and completed off post, and it strengthens continuing education, addresses implicit bias and racial profiling, and holds employers accountable for providing that training.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: This isn't just about protecting security officers. It's about protecting our constituents and our communities. De-escalation, in particular, can be the difference between a crisis that ends peacefully and one that ends in violence. We know, in every single community in this state, that security officers are providing an essential function protecting us and our constituents. If they are essential enough to trust with the safety of our communities, then they are essential enough for us to invest in their training, their safety, and their professionalism.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: I know many of them are here with us today, and we thank them for putting their lives and their safety on the line to protect us, and this bill will take critical steps to help ensure that they can be prepared and protected and given the proper tools to do their jobs safely and professionally as they do their essential work. That's what a SB 1203 will do.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: It has taken significant, significant amendments to put it in a place where it has addressed a lot of the opposition's concerns and will, again, put us in a place where we can know that the folks who are out there protecting us are prepared to do so. Respectfully ask for your aye vote on SB 1203.

speaker: Celeste Rodriguez
statement: Thank you, Assemblymember. Assemblymember Macedo, you are recognized.

statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in opposition to SB 1203. Colleagues, SB 1203 increases the cost of maintaining a license for security officers. That cost ultimately falls on office buildings, churches, and airports that rely on those guards. When the price climbs too high, those organizations cut back.

speaker: Alexandra Macedo
statement: They replace a person with a technology, or with someone who hasn't gone through the proper training and background checks a licensed officer has. This would lead to fewer jobs for the very guards this measure aims to help. Think about what a trained licensed officer brings to a post—years of screening and background checks, training in how to read a situation, deescalate it, and know the difference between a nuisance and a real threat.

speaker: Alexandra Macedo
statement: Judgment that comes from experience, not a script. They protect in big ways and small, spotting something wrong before it turns into an emergency and getting law enforcement there in time. None of that comes from a camera.

speaker: Alexandra Macedo
statement: A camera can record an incident, but it cannot stop one from happening, and untrained staff standing at the post doesn't have the knowledge base to meaningfully protect people or property. We know from experience when you raise costs on business, it leads to fewer jobs. This bill goes too far and will hurt the guards it's supposed to help. I ask for a no vote on SB 1203.

statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise in respectful opposition to SB 123. speaker: Josh Hoover
statement: When the price of that protection rises, taxpayers are the ones who absorb it, as public budgets stretch further just to maintain the basic security they already have. If this security becomes unaffordable, it puts public safety at risk. For these reasons, I ask for no vote on SB 1203.

speaker: Jeff Gonzalez
statement: So, they, they might attach to a, a business that is barely making enough to be able to employ guards.

speaker: Jeff Gonzalez
statement: And now, we have to also talk about the California burdens associated with that. Those California burdens associated with that leaves very little for the guard company to make money. How do I know that? Because I did it. So, I would love to have a conversation with the author, maybe the floor jockey, to, to look at this in a different perspective because it's, it's actually gonna hurt not only the entry level guards, but it's gonna hurt the businesses associated with that.

statement: I do agree that there's some de-escalation training that needs to be done, but I think that needs to be done at a, if you will, a tier two or a tier three level when the guard has been introduced into this above and beyond the observe and report. statement: But when we're just talking about a observe and report, I think we're, we're, we're adding too much of, of that in front of a very entry level piece.

speaker: Celeste Rodriguez
statement: Thank you, Assembly member. Assemblymember Ahrens, you're recognized.

speaker: Patrick Ahrens
statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise in support of SB 1203. In my district in Silicon Valley, security guards are needed and are so essential to not only protecting our schools and our businesses, but some of the most important technology in the world.

speaker: Patrick Ahrens
statement: And SB 1203 has basic principles to provide basic business standards so that these security guards get the proper training and employer—employer accountability—that we need to not only keep our schools and our businesses safe, but some of the best technology. One of the very first actions that I took in public policy and political organizing was to support and protect security guards in our technology industry.

speaker: Patrick Ahrens
statement: This is a commonsense bill. We're asking for basic standards. We—these security guards are on the front lines every single day in Silicon Valley, protecting some of the most important technology for the entire world for all of California, and this should not be a hard vote. speaker: Matt Haney
statement: Thank you, Madam Speaker and members. I, I want to thank all my colleagues who spoke, and I'm glad that there is so much agreement about how important, essential, the work that these security officers do. Again, I will note that some of them are here with us in the gallery and are watching, and they have told us. They have brought this bill forward saying that they want additional training to be able to do their jobs more effectively and deal with the situations that they are experiencing.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: So, they're the ones telling us that they need this additional training in de-escalation to be able to perform their responsibilities effectively, properly, and professionally, and safely for us—the situations that we are putting them in, in many cases in public buildings, in many cases in places that all of us frequent.

speaker: Matt Haney
statement: These folks are on the front lines of dealing with these issues and for us to do, do something as simple as, as requiring a little bit more de-escalation training is the least that we can do for these folks who keep us safe and we have determined are essential and deserve our support so that they can do their job with professionalism and with safety.
